title: Experimental and Data Analysis Workflow for Soft Matter Nanoindentation
protocol: Reconstitute PAAm hydrogels/cells following the Supplementary Protocol.
Start up the device according to the steps in the Supplementary Protocol.
Select an appropriate nanoindentation probe based on sample stiffness requirements.
Choose a cantilever's stiffness within the range 0.01-0.09 N/m for cells.
Select a cantilever's stiffness within the range 0.1-0.9 N/m for hydrogels with expected E between a few kPa and 100 kPa.
Choose the tip radius according to the desired spatial resolution.
Select a sphere with R = 3 μm for small cells like HEK293T cells.
Select a sphere with R = 10-250 μm for hydrogels.
Consult Figure 3C and manufacturer's guidelines to select the appropriate probe.
Follow steps in Supplementary Protocol to mount the selected probe on the nanoindenter.
On the software's main window, click Initialize.
Enter the probe details (k in N/m, R in µm, calibration factor) in input boxes.
Prepare a thick glass Petri dish with a flat bottom for calibration.
Fill the dish with the same medium as the sample dish.
Match the temperature of the medium to that of the sample.
Place the calibration dish under the probe.
Slide out the probe from the nanoindenter's arm holder and hold it in one hand to make space for placement of the calibration dish.
Slide back the probe into place.
Prewet the probe with a drop of 70% ethanol using a Pasteur pipette.
Manually slide the nanoindenter's arm downwards until the probe is fully submerged but far away from the bottom of the Petri dish.
Add more medium to the calibration dish if required.
Wait 5 min for equilibrium conditions to be reached in the liquid.
In the software’s Initialize menu, click on Scan Wavelength.
Navigate to the Wavelength Scan panel on the interferometer box to check whether the optical scan was successful.
In the Initialize menu, click on Find Surface.
Progressively lower the probe until a set threshold in the cantilever's bending is reached.
Check whether the probe is in contact with the surface.
Move the probe down by 1 µm using the y downwards arrow button.
Observe the green signal (cantilever's deflection) in the Live Window for changes in baseline.
If there is no change, increase the Threshold value in the Options menu under Find Surface tab from its default of 0.01 by a step of 0.01 at a time and repeat Find Surface step until contact.
Alternatively, bring down the probe to contact in small 1 µm steps until the green baseline starts shifting at each downwards step.
For softest cantilevers (k = 0.025 Nm-1), start from a threshold value of 0.06 or 0.07 and increase it up to 0.1 if necessary.
Decrease the Approach Speed (μm/s) in the same menu for soft probes.
In the Initialize menu, click on Calibrate.
Check the Live Signal window of the software to ensure that both piezo's displacement and cantilever's deflection signals move up simultaneously.
If there is a mismatch in time between the signals, lower the probe by 1 µm increments until the baseline of the cantilever signal changes.
Repeat step 9 if necessary after adjusting the contact threshold iteratively until the surface is found correctly.
If the cantilever signal does not change during calibration, increase the contact threshold and repeat the calibration from the beginning with a wavelength scan.
When calibration is complete, verify the new and old calibration factors on the displayed pop-up window.
Click Use New Factor if the new factor falls within the expected range relative to the liquid medium's refractive index (for water, n = 1.33).
If calibration fails or the new factor is NaN or incorrect, refer to the Discussion section for troubleshooting guidance.
Navigate to the Demodulation tab on the interferometer desktop.
Gently tap on the optical table or on the nanoindenter to induce noise.
Press the Calibrate button on the interferometer after inducing a full circle of noise by tapping.
Enter in contact with the glass substrate and press Calibrate from the Initialize menu of the software's main window.
Do not save the calibration factor.
Check again to ensure the white circle overlaps with the red circle.
Verify the calibration by performing an indentation on the glass substrate directly after the calibration as described below.
Load or make an experiment file by clicking on Configure Experiment and add a Find Surface step and Indentation step.
For the indentation step, use the default displacement mode settings and change the maximum displacement to the calibration distance (3,000 nm) to displace the probe against the stiff substrate.
Click on Run Experiment and check the demodulation circle in the interferometer window.
Check the white signal and make sure it is on top of the red circle during indentation.

Check the results on the software's main window in the Time Data graph, and make sure the piezo's displacement (blue line) is equal to the cantilever's deflection (green line) as the indentation starts in contact and no material deformation is expected.
Change the local path in the calibration menu by setting the Calibration Save Path to an appropriate directory.
Move the piezo up by 500 μm after successful probe calibration.
Load the Petri dish containing the sample(s) on the microscope's stage and manually move the nanoindenter's probe to a desired x-y position above the sample.
Manually slide the probe in solution.
Leave 1-2 mm between the probe and the sample's surface.
Wait 5 min for the probe to equilibrate in the medium.
Focus the z plane of the optical microscope so that the probe is clearly visible.
Perform a single indentation to tune the experimental parameters.
Configure a new experiment in the software's main window.
Click on Configure Experiment.
Add a Find Surface step.
Adjust Z Above Surface (µm) if the probe remains in contact with the sample.
Add an Indentation step.
Select the Profile tab and click on Displacement Control.
Leave the default indentation profile.
Click on Run Experiment on the main software window.
Configure the matrix scan to cover a sufficient area of the sample.
Add a Find Surface step with previously determined experimental parameters.
Add a Matrix Scan step for flat hydrogels containing 50-100 points.
Space the matrix scan points at 10-100 µm (dx = dy = 10-100 µm).
Click on Use Stage Position to start the matrix scan from the current stage position.
Tick the Auto Find Surface box to find the surface using set parameters.
Set the step size to at least twice the contact radius.
Ensure the profile does not violate Hertz model assumptions.
Leave the number of segments to 5, which is the default value.
Use the default displacement profile for setup.
Change the displacement profile if necessary, adjusting maximum displacement and time per segment.
Do not exceed strain rates > 10 µm/s.
Set the approach speed for the probe displacement toward the sample before contact.
Match the retraction speed to the approach speed.
For soft cantilevers or noisy environments, use an approach speed of 1,000-2,000 nm/s.
For stiffer cantilevers and controlled environments, increase the approach speed as needed.
Save the configured experiment in the desired Experiment Path.
Select a directory for saving data in the Save Path within the General tab of the Configure Experiment window.
Click on Run Experiment to start the scan.
After completing the matrix scan, raise the probe by 200-500 µm.
Move the probe to a new area sufficiently far from the first area.
Repeat the experiment at least two times for each sample.
Acquire sufficient data with at least two matrix scans per sample, containing 50-100 curves each.
Load the sample on the microscope as described previously.
Focus the z plane so that both cells and probe are visible at 20x or 40x magnification based on cell size and spreading.
Move the probe above the cell intended for indentation.
Configure a new experiment in the software's main window by clicking Configure Experiment.
Open a new window to configure a new experiment.
Add a Find Surface and Indentation step with default parameters in displacement mode.
Run Experiment to perform a single indentation on the surface.
Check whether the indentation was successful.
If the curve does not look as expected, adjust experimental parameters.
Add a matrix scan to the experiment if indentation was successful.
Configure the matrix scan with step size allowing for small area indentation at 0.5-5 µm spacing for HEK293T cells.
Adapt matrix scan depending on cell size to ensure tip does not indent outside the cell limit.
Run Experiment and wait for completion of the matrix scan.
Raise probe out of contact by 50 µm in z plane after matrix scan is completed.
Move probe above a new cell and repeat process.
Clean the probe following steps from Supplementary Protocol.
Switch off the nanoindentation device following steps from Supplementary Protocol.
Download and install software for data analysis according to Supplementary Protocol instructions.
Screen F-z curves to produce cleaned data set in JSON format.
Launch prepare.py from the command line on the lab computer.
Hold the shift key while right-clicking on the NanoPrepare folder and click on Open PowerShell Window Here if using a Windows computer.
Type the python prepare.py command and press the Enter key.
Right-click on the NanoPrepare folder and click on New Terminal at Folder if using a MacOS computer.
Type the python3 prepare.py command and press the Enter key to launch the GUI.
Select the O11NEW data format from the drop-down list.
Relaunch the GUI and select O11OLD if data is not loaded correctly.
Click on Load Folder.
Select a folder containing the data to be analyzed-single matrix scan or multiple matrix scans.
Click on it to highlight a specific curve in green and show it on the bottom graph (Current Curve).
Clean the data set using the tabs present on the right part of the GUI.
Use the Segment button to select the forward segment of F-z curves.
Crop the curves by 50 nm at the extreme left if L is ticked.
Crop the curves by 50 nm at the extreme right if R is ticked.
Crop the curves by 50 nm on both sides if both R and L are ticked.
Inspect the Cantilever tab for spring constant, tip geometry, and tip radius.
Ensure metadata has been read correctly.
Set a force threshold in the Screening tab to discard curves not reaching given force.
Manually remove incorrectly acquired curves using the Manual Toggle button.
Highlight specific incorrect curves by clicking on them and selecting OUT.
Save the cleaned data set as a single JSON file.
Send the JSON file to the computer where NanoAnalysis software was installed.
Launch the nano.py file from the command line by navigating to the NanoAnalysis folder.
Type the python nano.py or python3 nano.py command depending on the operating system.
Press the Enter key to execute the command.
Click on Load Experiment and select the JSON file in the GUI that appears.
Check the values of Nactivated, Nfailed, and Nexcluded in the Stats box.
Check whether the number of failed, excluded, and activated curves is reasonable.
Check the Raw Curves graph to visualize the curves.
Click on a specific curve to highlight it in green and show it on the Current Curve graph.
Change the status of a given curve using the Toggle box.
Click on the specific curve you want to change the status.
Click on either Activated, Failed, or Excluded to update the status.
The count in the Stats box is automatically updated.
Use the View box to change the view of the data set in the Raw Curves graph.
Click on All to show all curves (i.e., activated, failed, and excluded in the respective colors).
Click on Failed to show only the failed curves.
Click on Activated to show only the activated curves.
Click on Activated or Excluded in the Reset box to reset the status of all curves between activated and excluded.
Filter any noise present in the curves using a custom Prominency filter.
Apply the Savitzky Golay filter to the data if necessary.
Use a median filter based on computing the median of the data within a given window.
Inspect the filtered curves in the Current Curve graph.
Choose an algorithm to find the contact point (CP) from options including Goodness of Fit, Ratio of Variances, Second derivative, or Threshold.
Identify the contact point (CP) on each curve in the dataset.
Apply the selected algorithm to all active curves.
Adjust algorithm parameters to correctly locate the CP for your dataset.
Inspect a single curve by clicking on it and selecting Inspect.
Verify if the red line in the pop-up window corresponds to the location of the CP.
Check whether the parameter value (e.g., R2) indicates the maximum or minimum at the CP.
Repeat the process for all curves until the CP is located robustly for each.
Click on Hertz Analysis.
Generate three graphs.
Check individual F-δ curves with the average Hertz fit (red dashed line).
Adjust the indentation in nm up to which the Hertz model is fitted.
Set the Max Indentation (nm) to a maximum of ~10% of R for validity.
Check the average F-δ curve with error band and average Hertz fit.
Visualize the average Hertz fit on the Raw Curves graph.
Highlight each curve in the Current Curve plot when clicked.
Inspect scatter plots of E from fitting the Hertz model to individual curves.
Click on a data point in the scatter plot to highlight its corresponding curve.
Verify CP location by clicking Inspect button.
Exclude curves from analysis if necessary.
Check the Results box for computed mean E and SD (Eγ ± σ).
Ensure the computed values are reasonable for the experiment.
Inspect the Results box, reporting Young's modulus (E0 ± σ) for the cortex, bulk Young's modulus (Eb ± σ) for cells, and cortex thickness (d0 ± σ).
Increase the window length of the smoothing SAVGOL filter if elasticity spectra appear noisy with prominent sinusoidal oscillations.
Click on ES in the Save box to export a .tsv file containing average elasticity data, indentation depth, contact radius, metadata, and estimated model parameters.
Close the software after saving results.
Input saved results into another preferred software for plotting data and performing statistical analysis (optional).
Export graphs from the GUI by right-clicking on the graph and selecting Export.
Choose to export the graph in .svg format for further editing of font, size, line style, etc. in another software.
